h1:
Ayutthaya in 3 Days, 2 Nights
Temples, Palace & Riverside Cafes
intro: Ayutthaya sits just over an hour from Bangkok, but give it a single day and you end up speed-walking temples without really taking anything in. This 3-day, 2-night plan spreads things out: temples in the cool morning hours, riverside cafes in the afternoon, and the whole last day saved for Bang Pa-In Palace so you don't have to rush back. We've checked the opening hours and entry fees for every stop here.

blocks.html: The historical island of Ayutthaya is small enough to cycle or drive around with ease, and most of the major temples sit within a few kilometres of each other. So we set day one for the temples on the island itself, day two for crossing off the island to Wat Chaiwatthanaram and the cafes along the Chao Phraya, then close out day three with Bang Pa-In Palace before driving home. If you're visiting on a weekend, leave the first evening free in case the night-lit ruins are running.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Temples on the Historical Island

blocks.label: Day 1
blocks.title: Wat Mahathat, Wat Phra Si Sanphet, Wat Lokayasutha, then night-lit ruins

items.activity: Leave Bangkok by car, van, or train and arrive in Ayutthaya; check in at a guesthouse on the island and drop your bags
items.note: It's about a 1.5-hour trip from Bangkok. If you take the train to Ayutthaya station, hop on a songthaew or motorbike taxi across to the island.

items.activity: Start at Wat Mahathat to see the Buddha head wrapped in the bodhi tree roots — the image everyone pictures when they think of Ayutthaya
items.note: Open 08:00–18:00. Entry is 10 THB for Thais, 50 THB for foreigners. When taking photos, don't sit or stand higher than the Buddha head.

items.activity: Walk on to Wat Phra Si Sanphet with its three Sri Lankan-style chedis in a row — once the temple inside the old royal palace grounds
items.note: It sits right next to Viharn Phra Mongkhon Bophit, so you can pay respects to the large bronze Buddha in the same spot.

items.activity: Break for lunch at Pa Lek Boat Noodles, a Michelin Guide spot in the Tha Wasukri area
items.note: Open 08:30–17:00, closed Wednesdays. Bowls run 15–20 THB, so ordering several won't dent your wallet.

items.activity: Head to Wat Lokayasutha to see the large open-air reclining Buddha — far less crowded than the temples in the main zone
items.note: Free entry, great for photos in softer light. There are flowers, incense, and candles for sale at the entrance.

items.activity: If it's a Friday–Sunday night, head back to Wat Mahathat or Wat Chaiwatthanaram to see the ruins lit up after dark
items.note: The Ayutthaya Sundown event runs during certain parts of the year, Friday–Sunday roughly 18:00–21:00. Check the historical park's announcements before you go.

blocks.title: Day 1 tip
blocks.html: The temples on the island are within walking distance of each other, but the Ayutthaya sun is brutal. Rent a bicycle or electric scooter for 50–250 THB a day and tackle the temples in the morning and late afternoon, avoiding the scorching midday heat.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Off the Island + Riverside Cafes

blocks.label: Day 2
blocks.title: Wat Chaiwatthanaram, Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon, then cafes by the Chao Phraya

items.activity: Get to Wat Chaiwatthanaram early — its Khmer-style central prang sits right on the river, and it's the temple where people love to rent Thai costumes for photos
items.note: Open 08:00–18:00. Entry is 10 THB for Thais, 50 THB for foreigners. Costume rental shops around the temple start at about 200–400 THB per outfit.

items.activity: Drive over to Wat Yai Chai Mongkhon, with its big chedi you can climb for a view all around and a long reclining Buddha along one side
items.note: Open 08:00–17:00, entry around 20 THB. The stairs up the chedi are fairly steep, so wear comfortable shoes.

items.activity: Have lunch on the mainland, then stop by Mae Pom for roti sai mai — a famous old-school local specialty to take home
items.note: Roti sai mai is sold by the pack, 20–30 THB each, perfect as a gift to bring back — though it tastes better fresh.

items.activity: Cross over toward Wat Phutthaisawan and pick a cafe along the Chao Phraya, with riverside chedi views
items.note: This side has Sayama Cafe and small spots tucked under old wooden Thai houses, across from Wat Phutthaisawan — quieter than on the island.

items.activity: Wrap up the day at Baan Pomphet, a cafe and restaurant on a bend in the river with wide sunset views
items.note: Go in the evening for the best light. It gets busy on weekends, so book ahead or arrive before sunset.

items.name: Sayama Cafe
items.blurb: A small riverside cafe under an old wooden Thai house, across from Wat Phutthaisawan. Quiet and good for ducking out of the afternoon sun.

items.name: Baan Pomphet
items.blurb: A restaurant and cafe on a river bend, with an open wooden building and panoramic views. Popular in the evening.

items.name: La Loubère
items.blurb: A riverside cafe and restaurant decorated in European style, where you can linger over coffee with river views.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Bang Pa-In Palace Before Heading Home

blocks.label: Day 3
blocks.title: Check out, then visit Bang Pa-In before driving back to Bangkok

items.activity: Check out and grab an easy breakfast around the island before setting off
items.note: Bang Pa-In is about 20 km south of the island, roughly a 30-minute drive.

items.activity: Visit Bang Pa-In Palace, taking in the Aisawan Thiphya-Art pavilion in the middle of the pond and the mix of palace buildings in different styles
items.note: Open daily 08:00–17:00 (tickets sold until 15:30). Entry is 50 THB for Thais, 100 THB for foreigners.

items.activity: Rent a golf cart or walk the palace grounds, stopping at the Withun Thatsana tower you can climb for a view all around
items.note: The grounds are large and involve a lot of walking, so a golf cart is better value with a group. Dress modestly — no shorts or sleeveless tops; cover-ups can be rented at the entrance.

items.activity: Have lunch around Bang Pa-In, or head back into town for a meal before getting on the expressway
items.note: If you haven't picked up gifts yet, stop by a market or a roti sai mai shop on the way back.

items.activity: Set off back to Bangkok, avoiding the Sunday evening window when traffic tends to clog up heading into the city
items.note: If you're driving back on a holiday evening, leave a little extra time for traffic on the Asia Highway expressway.

blocks.title: Before Bang Pa-In
blocks.html: Bang Pa-In is a royal residence, and the modest dress code is genuinely enforced. Wear trousers or a skirt that covers the knees, and skip sleeveless tops and shorts. If you turn up underdressed, the palace rents cover-up cloths at the entrance.

items: Temple & palace fees — for everything in this plan, expect around 100–150 THB per person for Thais and 300–350 THB for foreigners.
Getting around town — bicycle rental is 50–80 THB a day, electric scooters 150–250 THB, or hire a tuk-tuk by the hour.
Accommodation — guesthouses on the island start in the high hundreds to around a thousand baht, with riverside hotels going higher. Staying on the island makes temple-hopping easiest.
Souvenirs — roti sai mai, woven-leaf fish, and Thai sweets from the markets. Buy them on your last day for the freshest pick.

faq.q: How many days should I spend in Ayutthaya?
faq.a: If you want to take the temples at an easy pace plus fit in cafes and Bang Pa-In, 3 days and 2 nights is just right. A single day is enough to cover the basics, but you'll be rushing and usually only manage the temples on the island.

faq.q: What are Bang Pa-In Palace's hours and entry fee?
faq.a: It's open daily 08:00–17:00, with tickets sold until about 15:30. Entry is 50 THB for Thais, 20 THB for students, and 100 THB for foreigners, and there's a modest dress code.

faq.q: Can I visit Ayutthaya without a car?
faq.a: Yes. Take a train or van from Bangkok into town, then get around the island by bicycle, rented motorbike, or hired tuk-tuk. For Bang Pa-In, which is outside town, you may need to hire a vehicle or catch a songthaew.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Ayutthaya?
faq.a: The cool season from around November to February has the nicest weather, so walking the open-air temples isn't punishing. In the hot season, do the temples at dawn and in the evening, and hide from the midday sun in a cafe.

faq.q: Are Ayutthaya's temples really open at night?
faq.a: At certain times of year the ruins are lit and opened after dark, as with the Ayutthaya Sundown event at Wat Chaiwatthanaram and the temples on the island. It usually runs Friday–Sunday, so check the historical park's announcements before you plan.
